theme: Longing, union, and love strong as death
readingInstruction: Read Song of Solomon 5:1-8:14. The mood becomes more complex, with longing, loss, and the great declaration about love in chapter 8. Read 8:6-7 slowly.
settingTheScene: The second half of the Song continues the cycle of love poems. There is delight, but also absence and search. The woman dreams of her beloved knocking at the door and then disappearing. She searches the city and is beaten by the watchmen. The couple reunite, and the poem moves toward its conclusion with one of the most famous statements about love in all literature.
observation: “I slept, but my heart was awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking” (5:2).
“I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone” (5:6).
“My beloved is radiant and ruddy, distinguished among ten thousand” (5:10).
“I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies” (6:3).
“Come away, my beloved, let us go out into the fields” (7:11).
“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave” (8:6).
“Its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD” (8:6).
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it. If a man offered for love all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised” (8:7).
interpretation:
Chapter 5 opens with a scene of near-miss. The woman is in bed, and her beloved knocks, but she hesitates. By the time she opens the door, he is gone. She searches the streets and is struck by the watchmen. It is a picture of the pain of missed connection, and perhaps of the way that love can be strained by hesitation. The daughters of Jerusalem ask what is so special about her beloved, and she answers with a long praise. Love is not blind. She can say exactly why he is distinguished among ten thousand.

The poem describes reconciliation. “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine.” The repeated phrase is a statement of covenant belonging. In chapter 6 the man praises her as “terrible as an army with banners,” awe-inspiring. In chapter 7, the couple expresses desire and delight in the language of the vineyard and the garden. The woman invites him to the field, where she will give him her love.

The center of the whole Song is 8:6-7. “Set me as a seal upon your heart.” A seal was a mark of ownership and a pledge of identity. She wants to be marked as his, permanently. “For love is strong as death.” Death cannot be resisted. Neither can love. “Jealousy is fierce as the grave.” This is the jealousy of covenant love, which cannot share its beloved. And “its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD.” Some versions read, “a flame of Yah.” Love is a spark of the divine. It is one of the only places in the Song where God’s name appears.

“Many waters cannot quench love.” It is the kind of love that endures floods. And it cannot be bought. If a man tried to purchase it with all his wealth, he would be despised. Love is a gift, not a commodity.

The Song ends with the woman’s invitation: “Make haste, my beloved.” It is a note of longing that is not fully satisfied. Love in this world points beyond itself.
connection: The words about love strong as death find their fullest meaning in Christ’s love, which defeated death. “Greater love has no one than this” (John 15:13). Romans 8:35-39 says that nothing, neither death nor life, can separate us from the love of God in Christ. Paul says in Ephesians 5 that Christ gave himself for his bride. Revelation 22:17 and 20 echo the final invitation: “Come, Lord Jesus.” The seal on the heart recalls Ephesians 1:13, where believers are “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.”
application:
If you are married, renew your commitment to your spouse. Say, “I am yours.”

Ask God to help you love with a love that endures floods.

Think about the love of Christ, which was stronger than death, and rest in it.
prayerPrompts: Thank Christ for giving himself for his bride.
Ask him to set you as a seal on his heart, and tell him what that means.
Tell him where you long for him.
